title: Nix
topic: Nix — reproducible builds, development environments, and declarative systems, taught from first principles
notes: The requester supplied a full syllabus titled 'Nix from First Principles — Reproducible Builds, Development Environments, and Declarative Systems'; use that as the cover subtitle framing. Central question of the whole book: how does a description of software become a built package, a development environment, or an entire system? Target audience: developers comfortable with a terminal, git, one programming language, and basic build/dependency workflows — no prior Nix or NixOS knowledge. Each chapter follows the requester's rhythm: (1) a concrete problem, (2) the mental model with a diagram or small example, (3) the smallest working demonstration, (4) under the hood — what Nix evaluates/builds/combines, (5) an experiment: change one thing and predict the result, (6) apply it to the one evolving project that connects the chapters, (7) trade-offs — what the technique does not solve. Editorial principles: teach concepts before abstractions; useful results early; examples small enough to inspect; always distinguish evaluation from building, and packages vs overlays vs modules vs flakes; debugging woven throughout; NixOS stays optional until Part V; make limitations, mutable state and operational responsibilities explicit; never become a syntax reference or a configuration cookbook. The evolving project: a small Phoenix (Elixir) service with a Rust companion tool, with database/secrets/persistent state kept explicit (capstone, ch. 21). The requester's appendices fold into cheatsheet.html (syntax + idioms, modern/legacy command mappings by task, glossary of derivation/output/closure/profile/generation/overlay/module/flake, common-error diagnostic checklists); installation/platform notes fold into the chapter 3 page; there is no separate appendix page.

concepts.title: The Problem with Software Environments
concepts.brief: Dependency conflicts and 'works on my machine'; hidden assumptions in install scripts and builds; recording installed versions vs describing an environment; introduce the project readers build throughout the book. Goal: understand the problems that motivate Nix before any syntax. Exercise: compare two machines that look identical but behave differently; identify the assumptions missing from their environment descriptions.

concepts.title: A Map of the Nix Ecosystem
concepts.brief: Nix the language vs Nix the package manager vs Nixpkgs the package collection vs NixOS the OS; where flakes, Home Manager and related tools fit; using Nix without switching operating systems. Goal: a vocabulary map that distinguishes the responsibilities of each component. Exercise: classify common tasks by the component responsible (language / package manager / package collection / user configuration / OS).

concepts.title: Your First Encounter with Nix
concepts.brief: Installation and verification (fold in platform-specific notes); running a tool without installing it permanently (nix run / nix shell); entering a temporary development environment; building a small example; inspecting what changed on disk and in the environment. Goal: a useful result before any machinery. Exercise: run a tool, enter a dev environment, build something small, record which files and environment settings changed.

concepts.title: The Nix Store: Software Without a Global Installation Directory
concepts.brief: Store paths and immutable build outputs; multiple versions coexisting; dependencies and closures; profiles, generations, and garbage-collection roots; installing vs building software. Goal: how Nix organizes software and tracks relationships between outputs. Exercise: inspect a package and draw its dependency closure.

concepts.title: Learning the Nix Expression Language
concepts.brief: Strings, numbers, paths, lists, attribute sets; expressions rather than sequences of commands; let/in, conditionals, interpolation; attribute access and set composition; reading a small .nix file top to bottom. Goal: read and write basic Nix expressions without treating Nix as shell scripting. Exercise: describe a small project using values, lists, attribute sets and local bindings.

concepts.title: Functions, Scope, and Composition
concepts.brief: Function definitions and application; attribute-set arguments and defaults; lexical scope; import and file organization; higher-order functions; common patterns like `{ pkgs, ... }: ...`. Goal: how Nix programs are composed from functions and files. Exercise: turn repeated configuration into a reusable function split across files.

concepts.title: Laziness, Recursion, and Evaluation
concepts.brief: Why unused expressions may never evaluate; recursive attribute sets; evaluation errors vs build errors; infinite recursion; tracing and reducing expressions in the REPL. Goal: explain evaluation behavior and the causes behind common errors. Exercise: build a lazy expression, introduce a recursive dependency, investigate in the REPL.

concepts.title: Derivations: Describing a Build
concepts.brief: A build description vs its result; builders, arguments, environment variables, outputs; inputs and dependency relationships; inspecting a derivation (.drv); writing a minimal build with no convenience abstractions. Goal: derivations as explicit descriptions of build operations. Exercise: produce a small text file through a raw derivation; change an input and inspect the consequences.

concepts.title: The Build Lifecycle
concepts.brief: Evaluation, instantiation, realization; dependencies as a build graph; sandboxed builds and undeclared dependencies; reusing existing results; sources, hashes, and fixed-output derivations; where reproducibility can still break down. Goal: follow one build through the system and name each stage's responsibility. Exercise: trace a build from source expression to output; introduce an undeclared dependency and investigate the failure.

concepts.title: Packaging Software with Nixpkgs
concepts.brief: From raw derivations to stdenv.mkDerivation; fetching sources; unpack/patch/configure/build/install phases; build tools vs runtime dependencies (nativeBuildInputs vs buildInputs); applying patches; diagnosing missing dependencies; package metadata. Goal: package a small program with the standard Nixpkgs abstractions. Exercise: package a small C program, apply a patch, inspect its installed output.

concepts.title: Composing and Customizing Packages
concepts.brief: callPackage and dependency injection; override vs overrideAttrs; working with a package set; overlays; the meaning of final and prev; fixed points through concrete examples; when an overlay is unnecessary. Goal: customize packages while understanding how changes propagate through a package set. Exercise: modify a package with an override, then the same customization as an overlay; compare.

concepts.title: Reproducible Development Environments
concepts.brief: Development shells and mkShell; toolchains, environment variables, shell hooks; editor and terminal integration (direnv); sharing an environment with teammates; separating application state from toolchain configuration. Goal: describe a project's dev environment explicitly and make it reproducible. Exercise: create a development environment for a real repository.

concepts.title: Flakes: A Standard Interface for Nix Projects
concepts.brief: Why a project-level interface; flake.nix inputs and outputs; lock files and dependency updates; packages, devShells, checks, apps; platform-specific outputs (systems); reading a flake without relying on a template. Goal: use flakes to organize and share projects while still understanding the expressions and derivations underneath. Exercise: convert an earlier example into a flake exposing a package, a devShell, and a check.

concepts.title: Packaging Real Applications
concepts.brief: Packaging a Rust CLI (buildRustPackage) and an Elixir application/release (mixRelease); language dependency lock files; native libraries and external build tools; dev environments vs distributable packages; when language-specific helpers are worthwhile. Goal: apply the build model to applications with language-specific dependency systems. Exercise: package a Rust tool and an Elixir release; compare their dependency-fetching and build workflows.

concepts.title: Testing, CI, and Binary Caches
concepts.brief: Defining build and test checks; running the same checks locally and in CI; binary caches and trusted substitution (cache.nixos.org, Cachix); remote builders; platform-specific failures; build time, storage, and maintenance trade-offs. Goal: extend local Nix workflows into repeatable team automation. Exercise: configure CI to build and test the same package readers built locally.

concepts.title: The Module System
concepts.brief: Modules vs packages vs overlays; declaring options vs defining values; option types and merging; config, options, imports, and module arguments; conditional definitions (mkIf) and priorities (mkDefault, mkForce); writing and testing a reusable module. Goal: understand the module system independently of a complete NixOS configuration. Exercise: write a small module with typed options and combine definitions from multiple files.

concepts.title: Managing a User Environment
concepts.brief: Home Manager; declarative shell, editor, and Git configuration; organizing reusable configuration; machine-specific differences; activation and existing-file conflicts; personal preferences vs project requirements. Goal: manage a user environment incrementally without replacing every existing configuration at once. Exercise: manage a small set of user tools and settings, then introduce a machine-specific variation.

concepts.title: NixOS: Building a System from Configuration
concepts.brief: Expanding package management into system configuration; services, users, networking, system packages; nixos-rebuild and switching configurations; generations and rollback; hardware-specific configuration; trying it in a virtual machine. Goal: how Nix and the module system combine to describe an operating system. Exercise: build and run a minimal NixOS VM, change its configuration, practice rollback.

concepts.title: Reusable Services and Multiple Machines
concepts.brief: Writing a module for an application service; sharing configuration across hosts; common policy vs host-specific details; managing secrets without embedding them in ordinary configuration (and why the store is world-readable); persistent data, databases, backups; reproducible configuration vs mutable state. Goal: organize reusable system configuration with secrets and persistent state explicit. Exercise: configure two machines with shared modules and deliberately different roles.

concepts.title: Debugging Nix Systematically
concepts.brief: Classifying syntax, evaluation, fetching, building, and activation failures; reading error traces and build logs; inspecting derivations and dependencies; reducing failures to minimal examples; debugging unexpected package selections; recognizing overcomplicated abstractions. Goal: a repeatable debugging method instead of trial and error. Exercise: diagnose a collection of deliberately broken examples and name each failure's category.

concepts.title: Capstone: From Repository to Running Service
concepts.brief: The book's evolving project lands: a small Phoenix service with a Rust companion tool — a dev shell, a packaged release, automated checks, a reusable service module, a NixOS VM running the application, upgrade and rollback; what remains outside Nix's control (database, secrets, persistent state kept explicit rather than pretending deployment is only a package-build problem). Goal: connect language, build system, project interface, and module system into one coherent workflow. Exercise: take the application from source repository to running service, then upgrade and roll back.

concepts.title: Reading and Contributing to the Ecosystem
concepts.brief: Navigating Nixpkgs; reading unfamiliar package definitions; adding or updating a package; testing changes; organizing a small package collection; reusing existing abstractions; knowing when to write less Nix. Goal: learn from existing code and make focused contributions. Exercise: update or add a small package and prepare the change for review.

images.prompt: An International-style graphic: flat geometric shapes on a white field, black and grays with one Swiss-red accent, strict alignment and generous whitespace. Reductive and rational — a diagrammatic image, no shadows, no gradients, no ornament. Subject: a single sheet of ruled paper at left, an arrow, and a solid block at right built from stacked identical squares, one square in red, suggesting a written description becoming a built thing. No text baked in. Target size ~1200×800px, 3:2 landscape; it is letterboxed into a 3:2 box, so keep the subject centred with safe margins.
images.alt: Cover art: a plain page of words turning into a built thing
